Nephrotic syndrome is top-ranked due to its hallmark presentation of symmetric, non-pitting (often periorbital first) edema and profound fatigue from hypoalbuminemia and possible uremia; it commonly presents subacutely over days. Acute glomerulonephritis follows closely—edema arises from sodium/water retention due to reduced GFR and often coexists with fatigue, hypertension, and urinary abnormalities (though not yet reported). Heart failure is highly plausible: bilateral edema and fatigue reflect volume overload and low cardiac output; early or compensated HF may lack overt dyspnea or orthopnea initially. Chronic kidney disease (acute-on-chronic) is included because decompensation (e.g., from NSAIDs, infection, or volume depletion) can rapidly manifest with edema and fatigue, but requires prior renal impairment—less likely without known history. Less likely diagnoses (e.g., liver cirrhosis, malignancy, angioedema) were excluded due to absence of jaundice, ascites, weight loss, urticaria, or airway symptoms, and the bilateral, non-acute nature of swelling."}
